Committee memo and available alternative

Memo: 'Online-only booking will save staff ten hours a week. Anything that saves staff time is the best choice for the club. We must therefore adopt online-only booking or accept permanent queues.' Further information: Fifteen members cannot use the online form independently. A partner organisation has offered two staffed booking sessions each week within its existing volunteer rota. No trial has yet measured whether those sessions could meet demand or how much staff time a mixed system would save.

The memo's strongest point is the potential reduction in staff workload, although the ten-hour estimate should be checked. Its conclusion depends on treating staff time as sufficient to determine the best option, without weighing access for the fifteen members who need help. It also presents two choices as exhaustive despite the partner's offer of assisted booking sessions. A mixed arrangement is therefore a concrete alternative worth testing, not merely an imagined escape from the dilemma. That does not establish that it will meet demand or preserve the claimed saving. I recommend a short trial that measures waiting times, unmet demand and staff hours before the committee decides.

Attendance trial at two fictional galleries

Gallery North extended Saturday hours in May. Its monthly attendance rose from 400 in April to 520 in May. It also began free admission in May, when a city arts festival took place. Gallery South kept its hours unchanged and attendance rose from 300 to 330; it retained its entry charge. A draft summary credits all 120 additional North visits to longer hours. There are no earlier trend data or visitor-level records.

Longer hours could attract people who cannot visit earlier, but the extra 120 visits are not an isolated estimate of that effect. Free admission and the arts festival changed the context at the same time. The relevant counterfactual is North's May attendance without extended hours, not simply its April attendance. South offers a possible comparison, but its unchanged entry charge and our lack of earlier trends weaken that comparison. I would seek several months of attendance and pricing data from more comparable galleries. Even then, I would state the assumptions and remaining uncertainty rather than assign the entire increase to one cause.
